questions.explanation_text: Gauss’ law for electrostatics says that the total electric flux through a closed surface is equal to the charge enclosed divided by $\epsilon_{0}$ . So, $∮\vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A}=\frac{Q}{\epsilon_{0}}$ Thus, (a) matches with (i). Gauss’ law for magnetism says that the net magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero because isolated magnetic poles do not exist. So, $∮\vec{B} \cdot d\vec{A}=0$ Thus, (b) matches with (iii). Faraday’s law says that a changing magnetic flux produces an electric field. Its integral form is $∮\vec{E} \cdot d\vec{l}=-\frac{d\phi_{B}}{dt}$ Thus, (c) matches with (iv). Ampere-Maxwell’s law says that magnetic field is produced by conduction current as well as displacement current. So, $∮\vec{B} \cdot d\vec{l}=\mu_{0}[i_{c}+\epsilon_{0}\frac{d\phi_{E}}{dt}]$ Thus, (d) matches with (ii). Hence the correct matching is: $a-i,b-iii,c-iv,d-ii$ Correct option: Option A.

Thus, (a) matches with (i).

Gauss’ law for magnetism says that the net magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero because isolated magnetic poles do not exist.

So,

$∮\vec{B} \cdot d\vec{A}=0$

Thus, (b) matches with (iii).

Faraday’s law says that a changing magnetic flux produces an electric field. Its integral form is

$∮\vec{E} \cdot d\vec{l}=-\frac{d\phi_{B}}{dt}$

Thus, (c) matches with (iv).

Ampere-Maxwell’s law says that magnetic field is produced by conduction current as well as displacement current.

So,

$∮\vec{B} \cdot d\vec{l}=\mu_{0}[i_{c}+\epsilon_{0}\frac{d\phi_{E}}{dt}]$

Thus, (d) matches with (ii).

Hence the correct matching is:

$a-i,b-iii,c-iv,d-ii$

Correct option: Option A.

questions.question_text: The total energy carried by the light wave when it travels from a rarer to a non-reflecting and nonabsorbing medium
questions.question_html: The total energy carried by the light wave when it travels from a rarer to a non-reflecting and nonabsorbing medium

options.label: A
options.html: remains same

options.label: C
options.text: either increases or decreases depending upon angle of incidence
options.html: either increases or decreases depending upon angle of incidence

questions.explanation_text: When light passes into a non-reflecting, non-absorbing medium, no energy is lost at the boundary. In particular: Energy flux is given by the (time-averaged) Poynting vector $\vec{S}=\vec{E} \times \vec{H}.$ For no reflection and no absorption, the tangential components of both fields are continuous across the interface: $E_{1}=E_{2},H_{1}=H_{2}.$ Hence the incident and transmitted fluxes are equal: $S_{1}=E_{1}H_{1}=E_{2}H_{2}=S_{2}.$ Since all the energy that arrives is carried forward, the total energy carried by the wave remains the same. Answer: Option A (remains same).
questions.explanation_html:
When light passes into a non-reflecting, non-absorbing medium, no energy is lost at the boundary. In particular:

Energy flux is given by the (time-averaged) Poynting vector

$\vec{S}=\vec{E} \times \vec{H}.$

For no reflection and no absorption, the tangential components of both fields are continuous across the interface:

$E_{1}=E_{2},H_{1}=H_{2}.$

Hence the incident and transmitted fluxes are equal:

$S_{1}=E_{1}H_{1}=E_{2}H_{2}=S_{2}.$

Since all the energy that arrives is carried forward, the total energy carried by the wave remains the same.

Answer: Option A (remains same).

If $I$ is the intensity of the incident electromagnetic radiation and $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum, the force exerted by the electromagnetic wave on the reflecting surface is
questions.question_html: Electromagnetic waves are incident normally on a perfectly reflecting surface having surface area $A$ . If $I$ is the intensity of the incident electromagnetic radiation and $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum, the force exerted by the electromagnetic wave on the reflecting surface is
questions.explanation_text: The force exerted by electromagnetic waves on a perfectly reflecting surface can be derived using the concept of radiation pressure. When electromagnetic waves are incident on a reflecting surface, they exert a pressure due to the change in momentum as they reflect. For a perfectly reflecting surface, the radiation pressure $P$ is given by: $P=\frac{2I}{c}$ where: $I$ is the intensity of the incident radiation, $c$ is the speed of light. The force $F$ exerted on a surface due to radiation pressure is given by multiplying the radiation pressure by the surface area $A$ : $F=P \times A=\frac{2I}{c} \times A=\frac{2IA}{c}$ Therefore, the correct expression for the force exerted by the electromagnetic wave on the reflecting surface is: Option A $\frac{2IA}{c}$
questions.explanation_html:
The force exerted by electromagnetic waves on a perfectly reflecting surface can be derived using the concept of radiation pressure. When electromagnetic waves are incident on a reflecting surface, they exert a pressure due to the change in momentum as they reflect.

For a perfectly reflecting surface, the radiation pressure $P$ is given by:

$P=\frac{2I}{c}$

where:

$I$ is the intensity of the incident radiation,

$c$ is the speed of light.

The force $F$ exerted on a surface due to radiation pressure is given by multiplying the radiation pressure by the surface area $A$ :

$F=P \times A=\frac{2I}{c} \times A=\frac{2IA}{c}$

Therefore, the correct expression for the force exerted by the electromagnetic wave on the reflecting surface is:

Option A

$\frac{2IA}{c}$

questions.question_text: Suppose that the electric field amplitude of electromagnetic wave is $E_{0}=120NC^{-1}$ and its frequency $f=50MHz$ . Then, which of the following value is incorrectly computed?

options.label: A
options.html: Magnetic field amplitude is $400nT$ .

options.label: B
options.text: Angular frequency of EM wave is $\pi \times 10^{8}rad/s$ .
options.html: Angular frequency of EM wave is $\pi \times 10^{8}rad/s$ .

options.label: C
options.html: Propagation constant (angular wave number) is $2.1rad/m$ .

options.label: D
options.html: Wavelength of EM wave is $6m$ .

questions.explanation_text: Given, $\begin{aligned} E_{0} & =120NC^{-1} \\ f & =50MHz=50 \times 10^{6}Hz \end{aligned}$ (a) magnetic field amplitude, $\begin{aligned} B_{0} & =\frac{E_{0}}{c}=\frac{120}{3 \times 10^{8}}=40 \times 10^{-8}T \\ & =400nT \end{aligned}$ (b) Angular frequency, $\omega=2\pi f=2\pi \times 50 \times 10^{6}$ $=\pi \times 10^{8}rad/s$ (c) Propagation constant, $k=\frac{\omega}{c}=\frac{\pi \times 10^{8}}{3 \times 10^{8}}=1.047rad/m$ (d) Wavelength, $\lambda=\frac{c}{f}=\frac{3 \times 10^{8}}{50 \times 10^{6}}=\frac{30}{5}=6m$
questions.explanation_html:
Given,

$\begin{aligned} E_{0} & =120NC^{-1} \\ f & =50MHz=50 \times 10^{6}Hz \end{aligned}$

(a) magnetic field amplitude,

$\begin{aligned} B_{0} & =\frac{E_{0}}{c}=\frac{120}{3 \times 10^{8}}=40 \times 10^{-8}T \\ & =400nT \end{aligned}$

(b) Angular frequency, $\omega=2\pi f=2\pi \times 50 \times 10^{6}$

$=\pi \times 10^{8}rad/s$

(c) Propagation constant,

$k=\frac{\omega}{c}=\frac{\pi \times 10^{8}}{3 \times 10^{8}}=1.047rad/m$

(d) Wavelength, $\lambda=\frac{c}{f}=\frac{3 \times 10^{8}}{50 \times 10^{6}}=\frac{30}{5}=6m$

questions.explanation_text: Given, intensity, $I=20W/cm^{2}$ Area of surface, $A=(25 \times 15)cm^{2}$ and time, $t=1s$ The intensity of light of energy $E$ is given by $\begin{aligned} & I=\frac{E}{At} \Rightarrow 20=\frac{E}{25 \times 15 \times 1} \\ \Rightarrow & =20 \times 25 \times 15J \end{aligned}$ The momentum imparted to a perfectly reflecting surface is given by $p=\frac{2E}{c}=\frac{2 \times 20 \times 25 \times 15}{3 \times 10^{8}}=5 \times 10^{-5}kgms^{-1}$
questions.explanation_html:
Given, intensity, $I=20W/cm^{2}$

Area of surface, $A=(25 \times 15)cm^{2}$

and time, $t=1s$

The intensity of light of energy $E$ is given by

$\begin{aligned} & I=\frac{E}{At} \Rightarrow 20=\frac{E}{25 \times 15 \times 1} \\ \Rightarrow & =20 \times 25 \times 15J \end{aligned}$

The momentum imparted to a perfectly reflecting surface is given by

$p=\frac{2E}{c}=\frac{2 \times 20 \times 25 \times 15}{3 \times 10^{8}}=5 \times 10^{-5}kgms^{-1}$
